newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Litany of leaks embarrasses Australia.
newsitem.headline: Litany of leaks embarrasses Australia.

text.p: The leak of a top secret Australian report scathingly critical of the South Pacific is just the latest in a series to embarrass the 16-month-old conservative government.

The Liberal-National government has ordered a top intelligence officer to investigate the latest security breach -- one of the most serious in years -- in which two AUSTEO (Australian Eyes Only) papers were left on a table in a public area at a recent conference of Pacific economic ministers.

One paper was scathing about South Pacific economies and the foibles of some ministers. The second was a confidential briefing paper to Treasurer Peter Costello ahead of bilateral talks with Pacific economic ministers.
But a string of diplomatic cables have also been leaked to the media over recent months, prompting the Department of Foreign Affairs to install a police agent at its headquarters.
The department has been ordered to tighten security amid concerns the leaks could discourage allies from sharing information with Australia.
The agent has been ordered to investigate 17 leaks since he was brought into the department in November, a departmental official told a Senate committee hearing last month.
None has been solved and the agent's original 12-month contract may be extended, the official said.

Some leaks have involved weighty foreign affairs matters, such as the recent publication by a newspaper of a cable from the ambassador to Cambodia, Tony Kevin, urging Canberra to work with strongman Hun Sen after he ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

Others are more gossipy, such as a recent cable from one Australian ambassador who recounted rumours of why an Asian diplomat was sacked. One cable was given to a Canberra newspaper journalist within three hours of being written.
Separate departmental probes into leaks of sensitive information have also failed to uncover those responsible.
"Unfortunately, most of them result in a failure to find sufficient evidence to take further action," Robert Hill, a government leader in the Senate, told the committee hearing last month.
Foreign Affairs is still looking at several other ways of containing the leaks, including reducing the number of documents classified for security.
Treasurer Peter Costello's department has been blamed for the latest security lapse at the Pacific conference.
Costello himself was embroiled in a row late last year over the release of information to journalists.
The treasurer, in a briefing with journalists, revealed details of a personal conversation with United States Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.
Costello's comments then about Greenspan's thoughts on inflation moved financial markets around the world.
